public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with an interior temperature/time optimum; excessive temperature or time may increase degradation. A useful first screen varies these jointly. I expect a competent condition to show high conversion but purity will require phase selection.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Under the dossier contact conditions, X0 should preferentially transfer target over impurity into organic (reported selectivity ratio 2.33), but one contact transfers only about 41% of target. Repeated extraction may raise recovery at possible stock/cost cost; organic washing may improve purity. X1 is predicted to retain most target aqueous and could be useful if the aqueous phase is selected, but separation behavior may be misindexed.

Decision rule: prioritize completed batches with final purity >=0.80, then maximize final recovery; compare numerical differences cautiously against assay noise and process confounding. A measurement in each batch will diagnose the reaction or selected phase before the destructive final assay.

# Campaign hypotheses

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
At 350 K for 1800 s, all four catalysts in S0 gave low conversion (~0.12–0.14 by HPLC; events runner-operation-0005, -0020, -0033, -0046). At 430 K for 3600 s, conversion rose to ~0.62–0.72 across the tested solvent/catalyst combinations (events -0059, -0072, -0085, -0098, -0111, -0124). Temperature/time are confounded, so this supports a hotter/longer regime rather than an isolated temperature effect. Safety observations remained below the 0.65 limit.

## H3 [supported within high-regime screen]
C1/S2 at 430 K, 3600 s gave the strongest observed reaction-stage combination: HPLC purity ~0.624 and yield ~0.448 (event -0098), higher numerically than other screened high-regime conditions. Its aqueous final material retained only ~0.263 recovery and ~0.611 purity (event -0106), so phase selection—not reaction alone—is now the binding problem. No replicate yet establishes precision beyond stated instrument noise.

## H2 [active test]
The dossier predicts X0 enriches target in organic relative to impurity. Previous organic selection used a poor reaction and only 0.01 L extractant, yielding low recovery and purity ~0.687 (event -0015); this does not disprove enrichment. Next, apply 0.03 L X0 to the C1/S2 high-regime product, keep organic, and wash. Prediction: purity increases relative to the matched aqueous batch (-0106), potentially above 0.80, at the cost of recovery. If purity remains below 0.80, intensify washing in the last batch rather than claim a qualifying process.

# Campaign hypotheses and final source-stage decision

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
The hotter/longer regime (430 K, 3600 s) substantially increased conversion relative to 350 K, 1800 s, but the factors remain confounded. C1/S2 was the best screened reaction combination: two HPLC observations gave purity ~0.625–0.630 and yield ~0.436–0.457 (events runner-operation-0137 and -0152), consistent with the earlier screen (event -0098). This repeatability supports the categorical condition choice within this campaign, not a general mechanism.

## H2 [not supported as sufficient purification]
X0 organic selection did not achieve the dossier-implied qualifying enrichment. One washed organic product from C1/S2 ended at purity ~0.664 and recovery ~0.100 (event -0147). Ten large washes catastrophically depleted target (purity ~0.008, recovery reported 0; event -0171), so repeated washing is not a monotonic purification strategy here. The dossier may omit other solutes/byproducts or its anchor scope may not apply.

## H3 [final decision]
No completed batch reached the required purity 0.80. Among nonqualifying fallbacks, batch 8 (C1/S2, 430 K, 3600 s; X0 contact with aqueous retained) provides the strongest recovery/purity balance observed: final purity ~0.611 and recovery ~0.263 (event runner-operation-0106). Batch 11 was purer (~0.664) but sacrificed recovery to ~0.100 (event -0147); batch 1 had slightly higher measured purity (~0.687) but zero recovery (event -0015). I will recommend batch 8 transparently as the best recovery-focused completed fallback, not as a claim that the purity constraint was met.

Unresolved alternative: a different phase ratio, staged back-extraction, or untested reaction/extraction pairing could potentially cross 0.80 without severe target loss; the completed design does not establish this.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic interpretation

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–workup system. The amount of isolated target is determined first by reaction conversion and selectivity, then by phase partitioning and losses during washing or drying. The assay variables are phase-specific: a downstream “conversion” value measured on a selected phase is not necessarily the whole-reactor conversion. This distinction is essential because, for example, batch 11 had reaction-stage HPLC conversion 0.726, but its organic final assay reported conversion 0.983. The latter cannot plausibly mean that extraction created additional reaction conversion; it describes the selected downstream material under the simulator’s instrument contract.

### 1. Reaction layer

A useful approximate decomposition is

`reaction target yield ≈ conversion × reaction selectivity`,

with deviations from assay noise, definitions, and additional species. For batch 8, HPLC conversion was 0.724 and selectivity was 0.587, whose product is about 0.425, compared with observed yield 0.448. Thus conversion alone is insufficient: conditions that consume reagent can still generate substantial impurity or byproduct.

The strongest observed kinetic relationship was between the combined temperature/time regime and conversion. All batches at 350 K for 1,800 s in solvent S0 had low HPLC conversion:

- Batch 1, C0/S0: conversion 0.130, purity 0.394, yield 0.051.
- Batch 2, C1/S0: conversion 0.134, purity 0.559, yield 0.071.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: conversion 0.144, purity 0.215, yield 0.024.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: conversion 0.121, purity 0.420, yield 0.033.

At 430 K for 3,600 s, conversion increased to roughly 0.62–0.73:

- Batch 5, C0/S1: conversion 0.617 and yield 0.259.
- Batch 6, C0/S2: conversion 0.669 and yield 0.332.
- Batch 7, C0/S3: conversion 0.642 and yield 0.188.
- Batch 8, C1/S2: conversion 0.724 and yield 0.448.
- Batch 9, C2/S2: conversion 0.695 and yield 0.171.
- Batch 10, C3/S2: conversion 0.677 and yield 0.288.

A plausible kinetic representation is

`dR/dt = -k(T,C,S)[R]`

and

`k(T,C,S) = A(C,S) exp(-Ea(C,S)/(RT))`,

with competing target and byproduct channels. However, this Arrhenius form is conjectural. Temperature and time were changed together, so their separate effects and any activation energy are unidentifiable. The data establish only that the 430 K/3,600 s regime was much more productive than 350 K/1,800 s within the tested recipes.

Catalyst and solvent primarily appeared to affect selectivity rather than merely accelerating total conversion. At the high regime with C0, S2 was best among S1–S3: batch 6 gave HPLC purity 0.485 and yield 0.332, versus purity 0.451/yield 0.259 for S1 in batch 5 and purity 0.301/yield 0.188 for S3 in batch 7. Holding S2 fixed, C1 was superior: batch 8 gave purity 0.624 and yield 0.448, compared with C0 in batch 6 (0.485, 0.332), C2 in batch 9 (0.273, 0.171), and C3 in batch 10 (0.505, 0.288).

This indicates an interaction such as

`k_target = k_target(T, catalyst, solvent)`

`k_impurity = k_impurity(T, catalyst, solvent)`

rather than independent additive catalyst and solvent effects. C1/S2 may stabilize or accelerate the target-forming channel relative to competing channels, but molecular identities are anonymous, so that interpretation is only a process-level conjecture.

The C1/S2 high-regime result repeated reasonably well. Reaction-stage HPLC results were:

- Batch 8: conversion 0.724, purity 0.624, yield 0.448.
- Batch 11: conversion 0.726, purity 0.625, yield 0.457.
- Batch 12: conversion 0.704, purity 0.630, yield 0.436.

These three batches support reproducibility of that operating region. Their numerical spread is compatible with modest process and measurement variation, but the campaign did not include enough independent replication to estimate a formal variance.

### 2. Phase-partition layer

For a single equilibrium contact, a conventional model would be

`n_org / n_aq = K × V_org / V_aq`,

so the organic fraction is

`f_org = K V_org / (V_aq + K V_org)`.

The supplied dossier reported for X0 approximately `K_product = 1.477` and `K_impurity = 0.635`, implying preferential target transfer into the organic phase. At the dossier’s volume ratio, the nominal organic fractions were 0.410 for product and 0.241 for impurity. This predicts enrichment in the organic phase, but not complete target recovery in one contact.

The experiments were qualitatively consistent with target splitting between phases, although not sufficient to validate the nominal constants. In batch 8, the aqueous phase retained after an X0 contact gave final recovery 0.263 versus reaction-stage yield 0.448, a retention ratio near 0.59. In the matched high-regime batch 11, the organic phase was retained and, after washing, final recovery was only 0.100 versus reaction-stage yield 0.457, or about 0.22. These values cannot be added as an exact mass balance because they came from separate noisy batches and batch 11 included a wash, but they show that a substantial fraction remains aqueous and that organic isolation incurs additional loss.

Purity did rise modestly when organic product was retained. Batch 8’s aqueous final assay had purity 0.611 and recovery 0.263. Batch 11’s washed organic final assay had purity 0.664 and recovery 0.100. Thus the organic workup traded recovery for enrichment, as the dossier suggested, but the enrichment was too weak to reach the required purity of 0.80.

The behavior also shows why partition coefficients alone are not a complete purification model. The dossier described only a target/impurity pair at specified anchor conditions. Reaction byproducts, solvent-dependent species, non-equilibrium transfer, entrainment, and wash losses may all affect the observed purity. X0 may genuinely favor target over one designated impurity while failing to separate other reaction-derived material.

### 3. Washing and workup losses

Washing was strongly non-monotonic from the standpoint of isolated target. Batch 11 used one 0.020 L wash after organic selection and ended at purity 0.664 and recovery 0.100. Batch 12 repeated essentially the same reaction and extraction but applied ten 0.040 L washes. Its final purity collapsed to 0.008 and recovery was reported as zero, despite a reaction-stage yield of 0.436 and purity of 0.630.

A plausible workup model is a repeated multiplicative retention process:

`T_(j+1) = q_T T_j`

`I_(j+1) = q_I I_j`,

where `q_T` and `q_I` are the fractions of target and impurity retained per wash. Purification requires `q_T/q_I > 1`, but even then target recovery decreases as `q_T^N`. The batch-12 result suggests either substantial target removal on every wash, a phase-selection or entrainment effect, or a regime in which later washes no longer preferentially remove impurity. Ten washes were therefore not simply a stronger version of one wash; they moved the system into a target-depleting regime.

The extreme batch-12 result also cautions against inferring monotonic process laws from operation names. In this world, “wash more” does not guarantee “purify more.” Operation count and liquid exposure are mechanistically important variables.

### 4. Integrated process model

At a coarse level I would represent final recovery as

`Recovery_final = Y_rxn(T,t,C,S) × F_selected(X, phase ratio, mixing, settling) × L_workup(washes,drying,handling)`,

where:

- `Y_rxn` is target formed relative to original reagent charge;
- `F_selected` is the fraction of target entering the retained phase;
- `L_workup` is the surviving fraction after washing, drying, sampling, and other handling.

Final purity can be represented as

`Purity_final = T_final / (T_final + I_final + B_final + …)`.

This explains the principal tradeoff. C1/S2 at 430 K and 3,600 s maximized target formation among tested reactions. Retaining aqueous product preserved more target but left purity around 0.61. Retaining and washing organic product increased purity only to about 0.66 while reducing recovery to about 0.10. Aggressive repeated washing destroyed recovery altogether.

### 5. Experiments that changed the explanation

Batches 1–4 established that changing catalysts at 350 K did not overcome a low-conversion regime. This shifted attention from catalyst screening alone toward a hotter/longer reaction.

Batches 5–7 showed that the hotter/longer regime raised conversion substantially and that solvent affected productive yield. S2 outperformed S1 and S3 with C0.

Batches 8–10 identified a catalyst–solvent interaction: C1/S2 clearly outperformed the other S2 catalyst combinations in target yield and purity. Batches 11 and 12 then repeated the C1/S2 reaction-stage result, strengthening confidence that it was not a single noisy observation.

Batch 11 changed the purification explanation. The X0 organic phase was somewhat purer than the matched aqueous product but lost most target, so nominal extractant selectivity did not translate into a qualifying process.

Batch 12 rejected the simple hypothesis that more washing would continue improving purity. Extensive washing depleted target so severely that both purity and recovery collapsed.

### 6. Scope and unidentifiable factors

The conclusions apply only to the anonymous materials, fixed reagent charge of 0.040 mol, catalyst charge of 0.005 mol, solvent volume near 0.040 L in most high-regime batches, stirring at 700 rpm, and the tested reaction and workup sequences.

Several effects cannot be separately identified:

1. Temperature and reaction duration were confounded: 350 K/1,800 s was compared with 430 K/3,600 s.
2. The complete catalyst-by-solvent matrix was not measured at the high regime. Only C0 was screened across S1–S3, and catalysts were compared mainly in S2.
3. Catalyst loading, reagent concentration, pressure, atmosphere, and stirring rate were not systematically varied.
4. Only X0 was experimentally developed in the final high-performing reaction. X1–X3 remain plausible alternatives despite their nominal dossier values.
5. Phase ratio was not systematically optimized, and no staged extraction/back-extraction design was tested.
6. Reaction-stage HPLC and final assays have different sample contexts and uncertainty models; their like-named metrics should not be treated as identical state variables.
7. Each final workup was assayed once, so small differences should not be interpreted as precise causal effects.
8. No molecular identities or hidden species amounts were observable. Claims about stabilization, protonation, complexation, or specific chemical pathways would therefore be speculative.

### 7. Plausible alternatives

An alternative explanation is that C1/S2 does not alter intrinsic selectivity but changes analytical response or phase behavior. The repeated reaction-stage HPLC results make a purely random explanation unlikely, but they cannot distinguish chemical selectivity from solvent-dependent measurement or sampling effects.

Another possibility is that extraction had not reached the nominal dossier equilibrium, despite 240 s mixing and 300 s settling. Emulsification, entrainment, or merging of reactor liquid with the aqueous phase could change effective phase volumes.

The low organic recovery could also arise from the wash rather than the extraction itself. Because no matched high-regime organic batch was finalized without washing, extraction loss and wash loss are not separately identifiable.

Finally, the failure to reach 0.80 purity does not prove that the threshold is impossible. Untested strategies—different extractants, altered phase ratios, several small extractions instead of one large contact, back-extraction, or a milder single wash—could plausibly improve the purity/recovery frontier.

### Overall conclusion

The best-supported process mechanism is a temperature/time-dependent parallel reaction network with strong catalyst–solvent selectivity coupling, followed by incomplete target/impurity partitioning and potentially severe workup losses. C1/S2 at 430 K for 3,600 s was the most reproducible productive reaction region, generating reaction-stage purity around 0.624–0.630 and yield around 0.436–0.457. X0 organic selection provided only modest enrichment and substantial target loss, while repeated washing was destructive. No completed experiment attained purity 0.80, so the sealed batch-8 recommendation is a recovery-focused fallback—final purity 0.611 and recovery 0.263—not a qualifying optimum.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate from the repeated C1/S2 results in batches 8, 11, and 12, while allowing wide intervals because the new recipes use 400 K, much less catalyst, different charge concentrations, X2, concentration, and wash staging that were not jointly tested. For Q01–Q06, the catalyst-to-reagent ratio is twentyfold below the campaign’s C1/S2 batches. I therefore expect limited target formation and very low recovery, even though organic selection can still give moderate purity because purity excludes material left in the discarded phase. Longer heating raises recovery in Q02 relative to Q01 but may also increase byproduct exposure. The nominal dossier makes X0 more target-selective and more strongly partitioning than X2, so Q03 is predicted above Q04 in both purity and recovery. For X2, decreasing organic volume in Q05 should improve enrichment but reduce target transfer, whereas Q06 should recover more target at lower purity. Q07–Q12 use only 0.002 mol reagent, restoring the catalyst/reagent ratio used in the successful campaign reactions and reducing substrate concentration; I expect materially better selectivity and recovery than in Q01–Q06. A wash is predicted to raise purity but lower recovery (Q08 versus Q07). Two staged washes should reject impurity more effectively than one equal-total wash, but with extra target loss (Q10 versus Q09), consistent with the severe cumulative wash loss seen in batch 12. Concentration is treated as modest impurity/solvent removal accompanied by a small target loss, giving Q12 slightly higher purity and slightly lower recovery than Q11. The 0.97 transfer fraction directly reduces recovery, and the pre-separation HPLC sample adds only a small depletion. Intervals incorporate final-assay noise plus much larger uncertainty from unmeasured kinetic scaling, concentration effects, phase equilibration, and wash-specific target retention.

payload.report:
1. **Status of claims and laws.** No explicit instance-specific mechanism or optimum was supplied. The only prior was the nominal extractant dossier, which was explicitly incomplete and potentially misindexed.

- The self-developed claim that a hotter/longer regime improves conversion was supported: batches 1–4 at 350 K/1,800 s gave HPLC conversion 0.121–0.144, whereas batches 5–10 at 430 K/3,600 s gave 0.617–0.724. Temperature and time were changed together, however, so a separate temperature law, time law, or Arrhenius parameter remains untested.
- A catalyst–solvent coupling favoring C1/S2 was supported within the screened conditions. Batch 8 gave HPLC purity 0.624 and yield 0.448, exceeding the other catalysts in S2. Batches 11 and 12 reproduced similar reaction-stage purity (0.625 and 0.630) and yield (0.457 and 0.436). This repetition materially increased confidence that batch 8 was not an isolated noisy result.
- The approximate relationship `yield ≈ conversion × selectivity` was qualitatively supported across reaction-stage measurements, but not as an exact identity.
- The dossier claim that X0 preferentially transfers target into organic was only weakly, qualitatively supported. Batch 11’s organic material was purer than batch 8’s aqueous material (0.664 versus 0.611), but recovery fell from 0.263 to 0.100. Exact X0 partition coefficients were not tested because the phases were not assayed as a matched pair under the dossier conditions.
- The stronger claim that X0 would provide enough enrichment to exceed purity 0.80 was contradicted by batch 11.
- A monotonic “more washing gives more purification” law was contradicted decisively by batch 12: ten washes produced purity 0.008 and zero reported recovery after a reaction-stage yield of 0.436. This changed the interpretation from washing as simple impurity removal to washing as a potentially severe target-loss process.
- Specific Arrhenius kinetics, equilibrium partition equations, wash-retention constants, and molecular explanations such as catalyst stabilization were modeling conjectures, not identified laws. The behavior of X1–X3, staged extraction, back-extraction, catalyst loading, atmosphere, and independently varied temperature or time remained untested during the campaign.

2. **Most informative additional experiment.** I would repeat the batch-11 reaction and extraction—C1/S2, 430 K for 3,600 s, 0.03 L X0, organic phase retained—but omit the wash before drying and final assay. This directly distinguishes the leading explanation, in which extraction gives modest enrichment and the wash causes substantial additional target loss, from the alternative that extraction or phase selection itself causes nearly all of the low recovery.

If the unwashed organic product had clearly higher recovery than batch 11’s 0.100, while retaining similar purity, I would attribute much of the batch-11 loss to washing. Recovery near the approximate partition expectation, roughly 0.15–0.20, would also strengthen the qualitative partition model. If recovery remained near 0.10 without washing, I would instead conclude that extraction, entrainment, or phase disposal dominates the loss and that the dossier is poorly applicable. Purity at or above 0.80 would show that washing was actively counterproductive; purity well below batch 11’s 0.664 would show that the wash did remove impurity despite its recovery penalty. Repeating the reaction-stage HPLC measurement would verify that an anomalous upstream batch was not responsible.

3. **Unused evidence and reliability limitations.** I used processed HPLC and final-assay values but did not inspect the raw spectral artifacts, peak assignments, replicate traces, or full uncertainty objects. Cost and safety observations were monitored but contributed little to mechanistic inference beyond confirming that the tested high regime remained below the stated safety limit. The dossier information for X1–X3 was not experimentally exercised, and the campaign did not exploit atmosphere, pressure, programmed control, catalyst loading, stirring, or systematic concentration variation.

The sealed batch-8 recommendation is limited because it did not satisfy purity 0.80; it was only the best recovery-focused fallback among completed batches. Its single final assay is less reliable than the repeated reaction-stage evidence supporting C1/S2.

The least reliable predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to a twentyfold lower catalyst/reagent ratio, 400 K, X2, concentration, transfer, and workup operations absent from the campaign. Q07–Q12 are also uncertain because the 0.002 mol charge, X2, wash staging, and concentration step were untested; the apparent contrasts within matched pairs are more reliable than their absolute values. Predictions involving washing, especially Q08–Q10, are vulnerable to the highly nonlinear loss revealed by batch 12.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. It encouraged broad reaction screening followed by aggressive attempts to cross the purity threshold, which produced useful evidence about C1/S2 and wash failure. It also caused the final batches to favor exploitation over a clean mechanistic control, leaving extraction loss and wash loss confounded. There was no clear conflict between the goal and reporting the evidence, but the goal reduced coverage of alternative extractants and independently varied kinetic factors.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch met purity >=0.80. Batch 8 is the best recovery-focused fallback among completed batches: final assay purity about 0.611 and recovery about 0.263 (runner-operation-0106), while the somewhat purer batch 11 recovered only about 0.100 and batch 1 recovered zero. It also used the repeatably strongest screened reaction condition, C1/S2 at 430 K for 3600 s.
